utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic, you're continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Antic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Yesterday we talked about your media appearances related to the 4th Detachment, et cetera. Now we're going to move on to another subject. It has to do with events that occurred between the end of 1991, all the way up to the 16th and 17th of April, 1992. So all of this has to do with that particular time period. Tell me: What do you know about the things that were happening in the town of Samac and around the town of Samac, all those things that, in a way, complicated the security and political situation in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, I know very well the situation in that period, that is to say, from the 5th of January onwards, from when the 4th Detachment was established as a regular unit of the Yugoslav army. Things were happening very quickly. Practically every day made things even more complicated from a political point of view and also from the point of view of the security of the town itself and the municipality as a whole. There was an increase in ethnic tensions that was expressed through the activity of political parties, through different forms of arming citizens for various reasons. Many incidents occurred, such as arson, various diversions, the destruction of various buildings, torching religious buildings, destroying transmission lines. In a word, all this threatened with the danger of impairing interethnic relations in general and also the danger of possible conflicts was looming over.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know about the following: That a civilian passenger car was being shot at, and in that car were persons who happened to be members of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember very well that something was launched by the SDA. Ethnic Muslims, members of the 4th Detachment, were called various derogatory names in this leaflet. They were called traitors. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, before the witness launches into this description of this event, it's not at all clear whether the witness was present, is talking from the point of view of an eyewitness, or whether he is relating hearsay, whether he has been informed this is what happened. It's important for you to know that particular aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The basis. MR. DI FAZIO: The basis of what he's saying, otherwise you can't evaluate what he's saying. So that should be clarified before he launches into a description of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic. I'm sure you understand the point the Prosecution is making.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity of seeing that leaflet?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the command we had this leaflet in our hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what was on the leaflet?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that members of the 4th Detachment who belonged to the Muslim people were called traitors, and they were called upon to leave the 4th Detachment. But this was only one of the forms of pressure against the members of the 4th Detachment who were not ethnic Serbs. There were other things that were happening. My men complained to me about all these circumstances, so I have full insight into what was the intention of this leaflet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Was any kind of ultimatum presented in this leaflet, in terms of leaving the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the end of this leaflet there was an ultimatum that, by the 6th of April, I think -- by the 6th of April, yes, that they should leave the 4th Detachment. We at the command, as we analysed this leaflet, believed that this was not too serious a matter, but the event that followed on the very next day pointed out that this was a very serious threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What happened on the next day?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Next to a coffee bar, in the evening hours the next day, a passenger car was driving by, and three members of the detachment wearing civilian clothes were in the car. I wish to point out that there were two Muslims and one Serb in the car. If necessary, I can give their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The members of the detachment who were in this civilian car were Mersad Mesic, who was a butcher in Samac. He was a very well-known person in Samac. There was another man, Nizam Ramusovic, who was also a member of the 4th Detachment. His nickname was Tota. And the third person in that car was Vitomir Danilovic, who is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know, do you have any information, as to who fired these shots at the car in which the members of the 4th Detachment were? MR. DI FAZIO: No objection to the evidence, but you have to know the source that this witness is relying upon to relate this to you. Is he -- something that he read in the papers, that he was told by people who were there, something that he saw with his own eyes? Only by getting that information can you then assess this evidence. But again, I have no objection to the actual content of the evidence; it's just the source that this witness is using to relate this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic, if you can lay the basis of his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have understood these instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How did you find out about the shooting, and who actually did the shooting?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since Samac is a small town, people find out very quickly about anything that happens. We found out about that practically the same evening, perhaps within an hour or so. We found out about this from the people who helped them at that moment. We at the command, as we analysed this incident, we asked the public security station in Samac to get involved immediately, to see who the perpetrators were, because it was not all the same to us as to what happened to our members. We at the command were duty-bound to take care of their safety and security. A few days later, the station informed us who the perpetrators were, and they said that the perpetrators, the perpetrators -- just a minute, please. Let me remember. Izetbegovic, Adis. He had been a pupil of mine at school. He is the son of one of the vice-presidents of the Party of Democratic Action in Samac. Izet Izetbegovic. The second perpetrator was a man by the last name of Srna. I think his first name was Safet, Safet Srna, also from Samac, also a member of the party of democratic action.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware of the fact -- actually, in what capacity were they acting then?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the members of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm referring to the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the Party of Democratic Action did patrol town. Very often they were armed. This incident also showed that in these activities they carried weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about what happened at the Valentino Cafe? Just tell me whether you know about it.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, because my apartment is right by that cafe. It's about 30 metres away only, so I'm quite aware of this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. That evening when this incident occurred, on the 14th of February, 1992, were you by any chance in front of the public security station of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment when that happened and when people found out about this event, people started gathering spontaneously in front of the supermarket, and the supermarket is right by that cafe. I noticed that for the most part, the people gathering there were ethnic Muslims. This gathering of citizens, it was a protest, in my assessment. These people moved to the police station, most probably wanting to establish the truth related to that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether you were there.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was, in front of the police station, with these citizens, and people were shouting out slogans, if I can put it that way, or actually, these were insults addressed to the Serb people, or rather, they were blaming the 4th Detachment for what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How did this gathering end?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After a brief period of time, the man named Hadzialijagic came out of the police station. I think his nickname was Coner. He was actually the brother of the father of one of those young men who had been killed. He spoke to the people gathered there. He appealed for tensions to calm down, and after a while the people dispersed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the setting up of barricades at the entrances to the town of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pisarevic. Before you move on to that question -- that issue, rather: I don't find that Mr. Antic has clearly answers the questions that you have put to him. On page 5, line 25, you asked Mr. Antic: "Do you know anything about what happened at the Valentino Cafe? Just tell me what you know about it." Mr. Antic answers: He knows about it because his apartment is right by the cafe. But at the time of the incident, pursuant to your other question, it appears that he's in front of the SUP building at the time of the incident. So it's not exactly clear. So if you could just clarify that before you move on to the barricades issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: This event -- you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Please answer, then.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I was not actually in the coffee bar, but according to our information, two boys, or rather, two young men, aged about 18, 17 or 18, were having fun and toying about with a hand grenade. They would throw it to one another and catch it. And at one point, one of them probably made a mistake and the grenade was activated. It exploded. And those two young men were killed. An ambulance arrived, which took them to the hospital, but afterwards we found out that they had died. When they were wounded and killed, another girl of Serb ethnicity was seriously injured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And just one little follow-up question: How did you, therefore, find out about it? You say "we had information." The question is: In order to recount this scenario to us, you should tell us where your information came from, being that, as you say, you were not present in the cafe at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, I was not physically present in the coffee bar. However, it was just under my window that the people had gathered, so that's how I found out about what had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Sorry to belabour the point. Last question on this: So at the time the incident occurred, you were in your apartment, which is 30 metres away from the cafe; you were not in front of the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. First people started gathering outside the coffee bar. I saw this through my window and I came out of my building. I saw the people gathered there. After a brief while, this group of people started moving down the street towards the SUP building and I joined them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: That clarifies it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: We're coming back to this incident now. Do you know that after the incident there was a gathering of citizens at the local cinema? Do you know who went to the meeting outside the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can speak about that particular event, because I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: My question -- previous question was related to the barricades. What do you know about the barricades that were set up at the entrances to the town of Samac in March?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the tasks faced by the command of the 4th Detachment, in view of its implementation and monitoring duties, we reviewed the security situation in the town, and we found out that during that period - it was a Saturday, more specifically - barricades had been set up at two entrances to the town of Samac. You can reach Samac from two directions only, two main roads, roads leading into the town. At the entrances to Samac, barricades had been set up by the SDA, and these barricades were mostly manned by SDA members. When we found out about this, we at the command reported to our Superior Command, and we were told, that is, ordered, that the 4th Detachment should not get involved in this, because it was no task for the 4th Detachment. We assessed the situation ourselves and we believed that this was endangering the safe flow of traffic and that it was up to the secretariat of the interior to take care of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before we continue, can I please ask the registry assistant to inform the people, whatever they are drilling, they are making a lot of noise for our proceedings. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how the barricades were eventually removed?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the afternoon hours of that same day, the barricades were removed. However, the event affected the citizens of Samac in a very negative way, because many people could not receive medical assistance. Many people could not leave town, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. All these events, finding out who the perpetrators were, and other activities that were being done, which of the state organs were in charge of all these things?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These tasks were to be carried out by organs, or rather, bodies of internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What do you know, and how did you find out about the arrival of two helicopters in the village of Batkusa, in the area of the Bosanski Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found out that in the village of Batkusa, which happens to be where I was born, two helicopters had landed, and that persons came out of these two helicopters who were wearing camouflage uniforms and they had their faces painted. A short while later, we found out that those were volunteers from Serbia. MR. DI FAZIO: Again, if Your Honours please, this is the sort of issue that it's, in my submission, absolutely crucial for you to know the source of this witness's information. He says "we found out." You should know how he found out, when he found out, who told him, what was the source of information, whether it was a document that he read, whether it was spies in the field, the activities of Mr. Zaric, or who knows what other source of information it was that allows him now to give this evidence. It's very important, in the Prosecution's submission, for you to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness has not even completed his answer. My question was: What does he know, and how does he know what he knows. So I think we should allow the witness to complete his answer first. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm sorry if my objection was premature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Continue, please. How did you find out about this? Who told you, and so on?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about this event from the locals. Anyone who comes along from Batkusa knows me or knows my family. They know me in connection to certain events. The following day, I believe, I had occasion to see for myself what had happened, because my father-in-law's house was actually a hundred metres from the football pitch in Batkusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us exactly: You say that you had an opportunity to see for yourself that they were present there. How did that happen exactly?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I drove with my family to the village, to visit my relatives. Outside the communal hall in Batkusa, the building of which I had initiated, I was stopped by two men with painted faces. One was standing on the one end and the other on the other side of the road. They looked at my documents. They checked the boot of my car. So I had a personal run-in, or rather, encounter, with these men.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any information from the command of the 17th Tactical Group or from your intelligence officers from the detachment?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, we did have all the information. As the commander of the 4th Detachment, whose area of responsibility was Samac, and Samac only, was in no position to take any steps with respect to that particular event.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you find out who met those people in Batkusa on that day?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed that they had arrived and at the same time I was told that they had been met at the football pitch by Stevan Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Did you have any other additional information about the people who had arrived at that time?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had information that, in addition to the volunteers who had arrived from Serbia, there were a number of citizens there from the area of Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know in what capacity they were there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard -- I merely heard; I did not personally witness this, nor do I have any information on anything that had gone on before, but I heard that those were people from the area of Samac municipality and that those people had been sent for training, over to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pisarevic. You asked the question, on page 11, line 22, how the witness -- or you asked the

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Tactical Group or from your intelligence officers from the detachment?" And the witness simply answered: "Of course, we did have all the information," but he didn't answer your question. Was it from the 17th Tactical Group? Was it from his own people, maybe Mr. Zaric, maybe somebody else in the 4th Detachment? So it's the same. And it also, with respect to your last question too, the witness simply says, concerning a number of citizens also there with the volunteers from Samac, he says, he heard, he merely heard, but he doesn't say how he heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You have understood the question?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed I have. I said my personal information, but we also had information that we had obtained down the chain of command, that is, the 17th Tactical Group, intelligence and security information. And Mr. Zaric, my assistant, had the same information, and he told me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who did you hear from about this group of people from Samac municipality who had been sent to a training programme?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the command, we were informed about this group of citizens. Mostly those were young people in their late teenage who had not yet gone to their regular military service, or a number of them who had already served in the army. We heard that those men had been sent for training. But personally, I had no information as to who had gathered them, who had sent them there, or who had trained them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who specifically told you that that group of young men had been sent to training, you at the command? Because you keep saying "we at the command." I'm asking you specifically. Who at the command told you this?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric is in charge of intelligence and security, and he was the one who always informed the commander about these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Which means you found out from Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from Mr. Zaric, at the command, I had personal information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the activities carried out in Samac municipality with regard to preventing the outbreak of hostilities and helping to allay the tensions? Who did you send to those meetings on behalf of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basic policy of the command of the 4th Detachment was to prevent ethnic strife and allay the tensions between the ethnic groups. We wanted at all costs to prevent Samac from war destruction, Samac, the town, as well as its citizens. For that reason, the command was very keen on attending all the meetings that were taking place throughout the local commune, meetings with whatever parties were organising the meetings. We always had our own proposals. We would always put forward proposals as to how the situation was to be -- was to improve. In terms of my personal duties at the command, I allowed Mr. Zaric to go to these meetings and attend them on behalf of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: After these meetings were held, did Zaric brief you as his commander about everything that had been discussed?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to everything that happened, Mr. Zaric informed the commander of the 4th Detachment. As a matter of fact, he informed us about events that were of a broader significance. But he also informed us about requests of specific political parties, notably, the SDS [as interpreted], because we were under great pressure, namely, that the 4th Detachment, as a regular unit of the Yugoslav People's Army, should be involved --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one correction in the transcript while the witness is still answering. It's on page 14, line 18. It was SDA, not SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps that can be corrected with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: The pressure you mentioned came from which party?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The pressure of the SDA, that the 4th Detachment, as a regular unit of the Yugoslav People's Army, should be involved in the newly established Territorial Defence in town. This was an impossible request, because Simo Zaric or I, or my superior, ever ordered me to do anything like that. So this was an impossible request that was put forth by that party. MR. DI FAZIO: Again, if Your Honours please, no objection, but I submit that you would be helped if you knew if the witness is saying that this was an ongoing policy or this happened at a particular occasion at a particular time, that the SDA adopted this view that the 4th Detachment be involved in the newly established Territorial Defence, whether it was a one-off occasion or whether it was an ongoing policy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Counsel can --

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'm going to put that question. Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: This request of the Party of Democratic Action, when was it put to the 4th Detachment, or rather, that the 4th Detachment should join the newly established Territorial Defence in town? Can you remember the day when this meeting was held, where this request was put forth?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish to say that the 4th Detachment was under certain pressure all the time, all the time. We are not talking about a given point in time or a single event. This request was the culmination in terms of what the 4th Detachment constituted in the town of Samac. This was put forth on the 16th of April, that is to say, on the eve of those events. It involved -- Mr. Zaric was very worked up when he informed the command of the 4th Detachment about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you say when this new TO was established, the one that the 4th Detachment was invited to join?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was, to the best of my recollection, three days before the events in Samac. I personally observed members of the Territorial Defence staff leaving. Some carried rifles. I saw one carrying a submachine-gun. They were carrying rucksacks and they were carrying equipment in tarpaulins on their backs. I saw that personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When did you find out who was appointed the new commander of the Territorial Defence staff and who was appointed Chief of Staff of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff of the Territorial Defence was a person, I think he held the rank of captain, and this appointee was Marko Bozanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What is he in ethnic terms?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: The other person?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other person was Alija Fitozovic, an ethnic Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: I asked you when you found out about that.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found out about that, I think, right after this Territorial Defence staff was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now we are going to move on to the 16th and 17th of April, 1992. You remember that night?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Did the 4th Detachment, or rather, the command of the 4th Detachment, take any special measures that night? Did you, as commander, order anything?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, as commander of the 4th Detachment, did not have any information that anything could be happening during that night. We had regular activities on the 16th. I already said that Mr. Zaric was at the meeting, and he informed the 4th Detachment, and we went home to bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what happened? What happened that night between the 16th and the 17th?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in my apartment. I was asleep. And at one moment, I heard occasional shooting. I mean, a gunshot or two would be heard, and then there would be a lull, and then the shooting would start again. I woke up, I looked at the clock, and I saw that it was 3.00, after midnight. When I heard that, I knew that something was going on. I called the person who was on duty by telephone immediately, because we always had a person on duty at the command. So I telephoned this person, this duty officer at the command, and he said to me, because he found out from our patrols that had been agreed upon earlier at local commune level -- well, this duty officer found out from this patrol that there was fighting going on in town. I ordered the duty officer to call the command immediately, the entire command staff to come to the Sit building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you come to the command too?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I came to the command. Most of the members of the command had already arrived. They came a bit before I did, because their apartments are right by the command, whereas my apartment is a bit further away, towards the Sava River. When we gathered there at the command, the duty officer gave us more detailed information, because the other members of the command did not know what was going on, because the duty officer had informed me about what had been going on. So he informed us about what he had found out from our patrols that were on duty during that night, every other night, for that matter, and they were patrolling our area of responsibility. When I found out about that, I ordered my signalsman to establish communications with the command. I ordered him to establish a link with my Superior Command, that is. He did that. And I informed my commander, Lieutenant Colonel Stevan Nikolic, about what was going on in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's just take it one thing at a time. Let's explain these patrols that you mentioned, that functioned on the basis of the agreement reached at the Samac local commune. What were their tasks, and where did they patrol, actually?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our patrols patrolled along the line of the area of responsibility of the 4th Detachment, that is to say, the right bank of the Bosna River, the right bank of the Sava River, up to the bridge, and some patrols also towards some important facilities, so that sabotages would not take place. These patrols had been agreed upon at local commune level. After an event -- I mean, I would call it an incident, when the military police patrol disarmed a group of SDA members. In order for these incidents not to take place any longer, all parties -- or rather, I don't know whether it was all parties that agreed, but anyway, agreement was reached at local commune level, and through our regular activities, we established these patrols and we gave them this assignment to patrol the area, in order to prevent any incursions from armed groups from elsewhere. But these patrols could also collect information for the command of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that the SDA also had its own patrols that were carrying out a similar function but within the town itself, within Bosanski Samac itself?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the SDA had organised its own patrols. I said that one of these patrols was disarmed during one particular incident. However, I personally experienced the following thing: The members of the SDA, all of whom I knew personally, followed me around town, everywhere I went.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And who disarmed this SDA patrol?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were disarmed by the military police of the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did the 4th Detachment have a military police of their own?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. According to its very establishment, the 4th Detachment did not have a military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before you move on: When was this incident where the 4th Detachment disarmed the SDA patrol? Was it between the 16th or 17th, or before the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Let's just clarify something: When did this event occur? When did the military police of the 17th Tactical Group disarm the SDA patrol?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was as far back as February.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So this was not between the 16th and 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: I have a question here. I beg your pardon. On page 18, about lines 24, 25, you talk about the patrols established by the 4th Detachment, and they were established in order to prevent any incursions from armed groups from elsewhere. What do you mean by those words "groups from elsewhere"? Were also, for instance, the so-called volunteers coming to Batkusa included in that concept?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: The Honourable Judge put a question to you. Let's just clarify this. Could you just clarify this: What were the tasks of that patrol? Did that patrol, for example, prevent the group from Batkusa from coming in?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The patrols consisted of three persons respectively. Usually they comprised two Serbs and one Muslim, or two Serbs and one Croat. Sometimes it was different. The patrols were not strong enough to act against any armed group physically. As the word itself says, they were patrolling the area. They were collecting information. They were observing various facilities, et cetera. That is to say that they were not capable of opposing any kind of armed formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Now you've given a more comprehensive answer, but you did say where the patrols did their work.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: But tell us: Did such patrols exist on the southern entrance into town and the eastern entrance into town? Where did these patrols go?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The patrols covered all of town, the entire town, from the south and from the other side, because the entire town of Samac was our area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pisarevic. I'm not sure whether Judge Lindholm's question has been answered in entirety, being that Judge Lindholm was asking these patrols, inter alia, were responsible for preventing any incursions from armed groups from elsewhere, and Mr. Antic has now said that "they were observing facilities, that is to say, they were not capable of opposing any kind of armed formation." So I don't find this very clear. If one of their objectives was to prevent any incursions, but they weren't capable of opposing any kind of armed formation, it doesn't follow. Maybe you could clarify it. It's not really making that much sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: That was exactly the meaning by my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please clarify this to the Trial Chamber: What tasks, specifically, did these patrols have? To oppose or different tasks? You, as their commander, what tasks did you assign to them, those patrols that were patrolling facilities, or the town in general, what tasks were they given? What instructions did you provide? What were they supposed to do in case of incursions by armed groups?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command gave these patrols the task to observe the lines of responsibility, to gather intelligence. But by no means did they have approval for armed combat or to get involved in any armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean, for example, that in case of an incursion by an armed group, they did not have the authority to open fire or to use the weapons, whatever weapons they had?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. They had no authority to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Well, I'm grateful for the answer, but it's not, so to say, in -- there is some kind of conflict between what was said by the witness earlier, that the patrols were responsible for preventing any incursions from armed groups from elsewhere. So this is now modified. Their main task was to patrol and report about what they had seen, not to take part in any armed combat?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please clarify the following: A moment ago, you said that their task was to prevent. What exactly did you mean? Is it what you've just told us?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Their duty to prevent -- the meaning of their duty to prevent, in such a case, with such developments, would have been to report the command of the 4th Detachment. The patrols could not take any action of their own, but they gathered intelligence, they gathered information for the command of the 4th Detachment; their members did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Let me get this straight. They would provide information on possible incursions by armed groups, or appearances of armed groups, and then report this to the command; that was all in terms of prevention, as far as they were concerned?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's exactly what the patrols did, in terms of preventing incursions by armed groups. They would simply gather information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A moment, please. I need to consult with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: The president of the Trial Chamber asked you a question that we have not yet answered. The question was: When did the patrol of the 4th Detachment disarm the patrol of the SDA? Did it ever happen that the patrol or the 4th Detachment disarmed any patrol belonging to the SDA?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The 4th Detachment never disarmed any patrol of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pisarevic and Mr. Antic. You did say that a patrol disarmed a group of armed SDA members. So if they didn't disarm an SDA patrol, they still disarmed a group of armed SDA members; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Maybe I can assist, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Because I was following here the transcript. I believe that there is one misunderstanding. What the witness said is that the military police of the 17th Tactical Group disarmed, and after that, a follow-up question by Mr. Pisarevic was whether there was any military police within the 4th Detachment, and he answered no. So if I understand correctly, those were not the 4th Detachment who disarmed the SDA patrol; those were members of the 17th Tactical Group from military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. I think the evidence was given along those lines by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So much for that question. Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Let's now go back to you, being at the command of the 4th Detachment at the Sit building. You told us that radio communication was established with the commander of what you referred to as your Superior Command. Can you please tell us: What was your Superior Command, specifically, the Superior Command of the 4th Detachment of the JNA? Can you please tell us the name of that unit and the name of the commander?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Superior Command to the 4th Detachment is the command of the 17th Tactical Group. Its commander is Lieutenant Colonel Stevan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Why did you call him by radio? Why did you use the communications equipment that you referred to yesterday as RUP 2?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used this equipment to call the commander of the 17th Tactical Group, because in the JNA, that was the usual way to get in touch. I can also add that very often in our town, the phone lines were down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember: When you were at the command, were the phone lines functioning?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: This RUP 2 machine, these were not Motorolas or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not Motorolas. Those were portable radio sets which a qualified communications officer carries with him. And then as soon as he receives an order, he establishes a link or communication, as ordered by the commander. It's the usual equipment used by our units.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us: What does it look like, this machine? If you could fill us in with some technical details. How much does it weigh?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It weighs between 7 and 8 kilogrammes. It's the size of a small suitcase.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Where exactly do you carry it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On your chest. It's attached to your chest. You have the earphone and you have the speaker.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Once you had spoken to the commander, what did you tell him? How did you inform the commander of the 17th Tactical Group, Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic, about what was going on in the town of Samac?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I conveyed to Commander Nikolic what we at the command knew. We knew that armed fighting was going on in town, or rather, sporadic fire. But as soon as you had the use of firearms, it was automatically some sort of low-level fire-fighting, focusing on a number of facilities or buildings inside the town itself. When I told the commander about this, he ordered me, as commander, and Simo Zaric, as my assistant, to immediately come to the command of the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. After you were ordered this, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We drove straight to the command of the 17th Tactical Group. We reached the command about half past 5.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who received you at the command of the 17th Tactical Group? Who met you there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander received us, but with him at the command were also his assistants, or chiefs of operational activities, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please remember any of the names of the people who were present when you met the commander there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Chief Brajkovic was there, and chief of intelligence and security, Maksim Simeunovic, was also present.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did you learn then? What did the commander tell you? And what further orders did he give you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as we entered the command building of the 17th Tactical Group, Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic told us that he had already been informed about what was going on, that he had been informed by Mr. Blagoje Simic, and that he had been informed that the Serb police and the volunteers had taken over the town, and that a Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac had been established.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What else were you ordered?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As commander of the detachment I received orders to mobilise the 4th Detachment. From the command where I was, I immediately called my assistant, or rather, deputy, Captain Jovo Savic, who had stayed back at our command. I called him and I told him to immediately carry out the order on the mobilisation of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask for some more detailed instructions from the commander, how you should act in this new situation?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As commander, I sought instructions, in view of what was going on, as to how the 4th Detachment should behave in view of the newly established situation. Commander Nikolic ordered us -- ordered me, rather, to go back to the command of the 4th Detachment, to mobilise the detachment, and not to start any other activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: You, as commander of the detachment, the 4th Detachment, how did you take such an order, namely, that the detachment should remain on the sidelines?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As commander, and as a soldier, I'm duty-bound to carry out the orders of my commander of the 17th Tactical Group. I had to accept such a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that regardless of your personal position, you could not in any way take any action apart from the orders of the commander of the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot take any action. I'm not authorised to take any action related to the engagement of the 4th Detachment if this went outside the orders of my superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And when you returned to Samac, to the command of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In view of the distance involved, we returned to the command around 8.00 in the morning, of the 17th, that is, and a number of members of the 4th Detachment had already gathered at the command of the 4th Detachment, because this is where their call-up locality was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me. With your permission, I would like to ask a question. I understand very well that you, as a soldier, had to obey the orders given by a superior, but you had, of course, I can assume, a personal opinion and a personal reaction. Were you surprised, taking into account that the task of the 4th Detachment was to defend the town of Bosanski Samac, that you received an order to do nothing, although both your commander Lieutenant Colonel Stevan Nikolic and you were aware that the town had been taken over.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you understand the question of His Honour Judge Lindholm?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So can you please answer it now.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an officer, it is my duty to carry out orders of the Superior Command. If some other order had been given, I would have had to take the appropriate measures, if I'm a responsible person and if I accept the Yugoslav People's Army to be my own regular army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: I shall assist you, so that you would give an answer to the Honourable Judge's question. How did you take this order not to do anything? As a person, as an individual, not as an officer any longer, but in terms of the objectives and the tasks of the 4th Detachment that you spoke about, that they would defend the town of Samac, et cetera, et cetera. This order of the commander, did it surprise you? Did it in a way not live up to your expectations? Did you find it hard to take in a way?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As person, I was hit hard by everything that was going on in Samac. The entire command of the 4th Detachment felt that way. In a way, this was not in keeping with the objectives of the 4th Detachment. We at the command wanted to prevent any kind of conflict, any kind of formations entering town. That is what I say as a person, as a human being. But as a commander, I had to obey the orders issued by my superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You said that you found a certain number of members of the 4th Detachment who had already come there. On that day, did you get a new order from the commander of the 17th Tactical Group, Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that first moment of mobilisation, about 100 members of the 4th Detachment came. According to our estimates, that is not a high call-up response percentage. However, at that moment, many of our members were out of town; others could not have been informed; some simply did not dare leave their houses, out of fear. So that is my explanation for why so few people showed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us a percentage as to how many members of the 4th Detachment responded to call-up?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the 4th Detachment had 450 members, if 100 appeared, a bit over a hundred, then that's about 25 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, since you are an officer, when a unit is mobilised according to these military criteria, when is this mobilisation considered to be successful, according to military criteria?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to military standards, any call-up response that goes below 95 per cent is considered to be unsuccessful.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: It is your assessment that this was unsuccessful, the call-up response, the mobilisation of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, it was unsuccessful. However, in view of the number of members of the 4th Detachment, the 4th Detachment did have to carry out its task.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So what kind of orders did you receive, if any, from Commander Nikolic, from the 17th Tactical Group, and when did this happen, if so?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What followed soon was an order of the commander of the 17th Tactical Group, Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic. This was around 9.00. The order said that the 4th Detachment should go to the line of its area of responsibility, and that is the right bank of the Sava River, from the bridge to the mouth of the Bosna River into the Sava, and also the right bank of the Bosna River.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Are those the embankments protecting the town of Samac from floods?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are embankments. When the water level is high, then they protect Samac, because its level is practically below the level of the water. So it is these embankments that protect the town from floods.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did you do, as commander, after you received such orders?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As commander, I personally took the members of my detachment to the line, or rather, to these embankments. As the members of the 4th Detachment were being deployed along this line, we had our first combat experience; namely, one of our members was seriously wounded by sniper fire from a position on the other side of the Sava River, that is to say, from the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When did you manage to get the 4th Detachment to this borderline of the area of responsibility of the detachment, and also of the town itself?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the day, our members -- other members of our detachment kept coming in, those who were informed about the mobilisation, and until the evening -- by the evening hours, we managed to get to this defence line.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Parallel to that, did the 4th Detachment take any other measures? If so, tell us what was done and in what way, and so on.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every combat unit and every command has to take care of their members in situation of combat. Right by the embankment, there are apartment buildings where citizens of Samac live. We were ordered that the command should secure the rear of its ranks. Therefore, in that zone - this is only about ten metres or less behind us - we took all measures to collect weapons from citizens who illegally possessed weapons. We were afraid that there might be casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that this would be the right moment to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll continue at 1100 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before we proceed with the evidence, the Trial Chamber has been informed that the accused Mr. Simo Zaric has an appointment with the doctor, in which case, he wouldn't be able to sit in the afternoon, because otherwise it will be late for him. In those circumstances, we will proceed with our normal programme and continue with our proceedings up to 1345 hours. Mr. Pisarevic, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Before the break, we spoke about the collection of arms and weapons. Tell us, please: Which specific orders did you give regarding the collection of weapons? How was that to be done? Can you tell us about it, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My order regarding the collection of weapons was very decided. It was that while weapons were being collected, citizens were not to be put under any kind of pressure. The order was that weapons would be collected only from those citizens who decided to hand over their weapons of their own free will. It was not allowed to enter residential buildings, flats, or private houses. Weapons were to be collected in such a way that citizens would bring their weapons outside, to a collection point or to their own garden, and then members of our detachment were to collect these weapons and proceed in keeping with their orders. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, you would be able to understand this better if you knew where this order came from. The witness has said -- it's gone off my screen now, but: We were ordered and then went on to describe something about the collection of weapons. And then has said at page 32, line 2: "My order regarding the collection of weapons was very decided." Just so that the Chamber is clear, we should know where this order for collection of weapons came from; namely, whether it was from further up in the command or whether it emanated from this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm sure counsel will be able to clear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You've explained how this collection of weapons was done and what the reasons were. Where did you receive the order from to collect automatic weapons?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got this order from the command of the 17th Tactical Group, and I forwarded this order and provided detailed instructions as to how I had received this order from the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. How long did this collection of weapons go on for? How many days?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This began on the 17th, in the afternoon, and was continued on the 18th. Because on the 17th, we first took up defence positions along our line of defence, towards the River Bosna. On that afternoon, positions were taken up along the embankment on the River Sava, and then we spread towards the line of defence and in an even broader area on the following day, that is, the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you issue any instructions regarding the control of this activity? How was it done exactly?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally, the order also said -- that is, I specified who would be in control of that. I personally controlled that. But this was being done in a broader area. So I gave the same orders to Mr. Zaric and to Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any violations of this order of yours? Did you receive any information concerning possible violations? And would you have known had there been any violations of your order?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This collection of weapons went smoothly, without a single incident. I'm able to say that, to confirm that, because no citizens came complaining about anyone acting in a way contrary to my orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the order, exactly? Where were these collected weapons to be stored and handed over?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the order, I also instructed Mr. Tadic, as the logistics officer, together with the list of the weapons collected, and I believe that we managed to collect about a hundred different pieces. So in addition to this list, this was handed over to the warehouse at the TO staff building, across the road from the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You said that various kinds of weapons had been collected. What specific weapons?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of those were long-barrel weapons owned by citizens for various reasons. A number of hunting weapons were also handed over. There were carabines. Citizens believed that that was what they should do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were there any automatic weapons that people were not allowed to keep?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were a number of automatic weapons, rifles. According to regulations, citizens were not allowed to keep those.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Once you had taken members of the 4th Detachment to the line in those areas, during that night, did you issue any orders regarding insignia?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were supposed to take care of the safety and security of all our members. So from our superior commander, we received orders that we should in some way mark off our own members, give them distinctive marks, on the 17th, in the evening, because during the night there was supposed to be a changeover of shift. And this would be done in order to avoid clashes with police members who were patrolling the town. We decided to make our members wear white armbands, which they would wear on the left or right shoulder strap, or on their sleeve.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us whether all members of the 4th Detachment were wearing JNA uniforms, or were there also members of the 4th Detachment who were not wearing JNA uniforms?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely because a significant, considerable number of members of the 4th Detachment had not signed for regular uniforms, they would go to their shift wearing their civilian clothes and carrying military weapons. That's exactly why there was a likelihood of an incident taking place, and that was precisely why we decided to give our own members distinctive marks to wear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: People in civilian clothes, members of the 4th Detachment, where were they placed, this band?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wear this band, this armband, on their upper left arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What occurred the next day, on the 18th of April, 1992? Did the command take any steps regarding the command post and so on?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We at the command assessed the situation and came to the conclusion that in view of what was happening, it was no longer safe for the command to remain at the Sit building, which was a prefab building. So a simple shell, a simple mortar shell, could destroy the building and cause a tragedy or, rather, casualties among the members of the command. We took a number of steps to move the command of the 4th Detachment to a different location. We found a building that we believed was suitable. It was a very solid building and it had a reliable shelter. This was a building belonging to a Serb named Dusanovic, Jovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Was this building in a part of town usually referred to as Sljivak [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. The distance between the original command post and the new one is between three and four hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pisarevic, before you move on. I just want to clarify one thing with Mr. Antic. Just before we had our break, Mr. Antic mentioned, on page 31, line 7, and I'll quote. He said: "We took all measures to collect weapons from citizens who illegally possessed them." And now after the break -- he's obviously talked in more detail about weapons, but I don't seem to now see any reference to the adjective "illegal." So my question, for clarification, is: Was it only illegally possessed weapons that the 4th Detachment was ordered to collect from citizens in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, you understood the question?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The precise wording of the order was to collect illegally possessed weapons, illegally possessed weapons. However, there were a number of citizens who were in legal possession of weapons but still decided to turn it over. We did not refuse to collect such weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you say "legally possessed," what exactly does that mean, according to the regulations?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Legal or lawful possession of a weapon is only in such cases where the secretariat of the interior has issued a special approval or permit. This is usually about short-barreled weapons, meaning a handgun or hunting weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: As you were the chief of the SUP, can you please clarify to the Trial Chamber: Did the secretariat of the interior in any way have the authority to issue permits for the possession of automatic military weapons? Was that possible at all?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the law governing the work of the secretariat of the interior, no such permit could be issued, military weapons. The secretariat certainly did not have the authority to authorise possession of automatic military weapons, and citizens were not allowed to keep those.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: In practical terms, does that mean that every person who owned automatic military weapons owned these weapons illegally or unlawfully, with the exception of members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You, as commander, on the 18th, did you have any contact with the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Samac? Did you entertain any kind of contact, and with whom, basically, on that particular day and over the following days?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As commander of the 4th Detachment, in those days I had no contact with the Crisis Staff, nor did the Crisis Staff ever get in touch with me. Throughout that period, my only contacts were with my superior commander, the commander of the 17th Tactical Group, Lieutenant Colonel Stevan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. If you can please tell us, if you can remember: Did you ever hear about any announcement published by the Crisis Staff of Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about the announcement and about its contents over the Bosanski Samac local radio station. This was an announcement by the Crisis Staff that was published, I believe, on the 18th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you heard the announcement, what was your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The announcement was about the following: Every citizen was supposed to comply with orders issued by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. What was the overall situation? What information did you have as to what was going on in the town of Samac? Were people being arrested and so on?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have quite a lot of information regarding the situation in Samac, primarily regarding expropriation of property or misappropriation of property belonging to citizens of Samac regarding citizens' vehicles being seized, machines or property in. There were many cases of abuse and maltreatment of citizens. In one word, the tensions were high. There were also a number of cases where weapons had been taken from members of the 4th Detachment, by my own unit. Some arrests were made later on. They were arrested and they were taken away from the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that. Who carried out these arrests in the town of Samac?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arrests were carried out by members of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of a single case of the members of the 4th Detachment or members of the Yugoslav People's Army having arrested a single person in the town of Samac?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assert with full responsibility that not a single member of my detachment took part in any incident whatsoever or could have any one of my members arrested any citizens in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did you do when you found out that certain members of the 4th Detachment had their weapons taken away from them and that they were detained at the police station in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were -- we felt very bad about this, because we knew that members of the police could not arrest soldiers of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you inform the commander of the 17th Tactical Group, Commander Nikolic, about that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, especially along security lines, Mr. Zaric reported to his superior about these cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And were these members of the 4th Detachment finally released?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were cases that they were released and there were cases when they were detained further, to reasons that were inexplicable to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pisarevic. Just to clarify something. Mr. Antic, you are saying here that some members of the 4th Detachment were arrested and taken to the police station in Bosanski Samac, but you said a little bit earlier, on page 38, lines 13 to 15, that "there were a number of cases where weapons had been taken from members of the 4th Detachment by my own unit." I'm uncertain as to what "by my own unit" means or whether it's simply an error in translation. Do you think you could clarify that, Mr. Pisarevic? Because by the way -- from the way it reads right now, it sounds as though members of the 4th Detachment were arresting other members of the 4th Detachment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There was probably a misinterpretation, because that's not the way the witness had put it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: I think you were talking about weapons being taken away from the members of the 4th Detachment. So could you please use these adjectives less -- I mean "my," "mine," et cetera, would you just say "members of the 4th Detachment" so that we can be clear.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the police took away weapons, army weapons, from members of the 4th Detachment, for which they had appropriate documents, permits for carrying such army weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Some members of the 4th Detachment were detained; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some members of the 4th Detachment were detained. So out of a feeling of personal protest, I went to prison myself and took them out personally, until I was told at one point in time that I could personally lose my life due to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: If you permit me, I have another question about the point which is a bit unclear to me. You said that -- or the witness confirmed that arrests were carried out in the town of Samac, not only referring to members of the 4th Detachment but arrests in general, and as an answer to your question, the witness said, word by word -- it's on page 38, line 19: "Arrests were carried out by members of the police." What do you exactly mean by those words "members of the police"? Who were those carrying out those arrests?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you understand the question put by the Honourable Judge?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Members of the police were persons wearing police uniforms. So they were members of the organs of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: If I may put a follow-up question. So when you are talking about members of the police, those are members of the police already in that position before the outbreak of the hostilities, or are they -- do you mean people taking on police uniforms after what happened during the night between the 16th and 17th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A number of members of the police were from the peacetime period, and another number of police members - I don't know how many - were engaged in the police after these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Was this a new police, in essence? And whose was it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the police that was the organ of the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who was the chief of that police?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of that police was Mr. Stevan Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you spoke a short while ago about detentions, about appropriation of property, et cetera, who was it that was doing this?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was being done by volunteers from Serbia, for the most part, but also by members of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, under whose command were these volunteers from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of our knowledge, the volunteers from Serbia were under the leadership of the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who was personally and directly their superior?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The organ of the civilian authorities that led or, rather, carried out authority was the civilian authority of the municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So that was the organ. But who was the person commanding these persons? Were they within the police or were they within the Yugoslav People's Army or were they within some third formation, if any?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These volunteers were not under any command of the army. They had nothing to do with the army. They were supposed to be, supposed to be, under the leadership and control of the authorities of the interior, and the chief of the interior was Stevan Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: So, in fact, that maybe answers the question, but just to make sure: Mr. Antic, you were saying that these volunteers from Serbia were under the leadership of the civilian authorities. And if I understand you now correctly, you're saying the civilian authorities were in the form of Mr. Todorovic. Is that correct? Civilian -- by "civilian authorities," are you talking about the police authorities or are you talking about other civilian authorities in Bosanski Samac? I think it's an important point. We need to get it clearly what you actually mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You have heard the question put by Judge Williams. Please tell us whether, for you, the police is the civilian authority that you've been referring to. When you say "the civilian authority," are you referring to the police?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to all regulations, the police is the organ of civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So when you say this was under the command of the civilian authorities, you mean that it was under the command of the police; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Since you said a while ago that the situation was very tense and very complex, what did you, as the commander of the 4th Detachment, and what did the command of the 4th Detachment do, and did you, in a way, address the citizens of Bosanski Samac? Did you address them by way of a proclamation or something?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the developments in Samac, in view of all these events that I have been speaking about, the command of the 4th Detachment had a totally negative attitude. We thought that this was impermissible, and therefore, in the command of the 4th Detachment, we decided to address the citizens, asking them to join us, as many of them as they could, not to be deceived by various provocations, and simply to make it possible to resolve certain situations in a positive sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please put before the witness D21/4 ter. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, while that's being done, I raise this issue with you: The witness has just said that "the view of the 4th Detachment was that all of these events were impermissible." Now, you might like to know what he's referring to. Is he referring to arrests of the 4th Detachment only, arrests generally, the political events, if you want to call them that, that occurred on the night of the 16th or 17th? What did the 4th Detachment think was impermissible? A little precision in that might be useful to you in order for you to understand this witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm sure that the witness has heard what the Prosecutor has said, so he can go ahead and explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, could you please answer.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN ANTIC [Resumed]
